title: Fidelis EDR Deployment Strategy for Unmanaged and Remote Endpoints
summary: Key Takeaways Remote and unmanaged endpoints create major visibility gaps that attackers actively exploit through credential theft, fileless malware, and LOTL techniques. Fidelis EDR delivers on-device behavioral detection without VPN dependency, maintaining visibility even when endpoints are off-network. The Endpoint Collector enables 90-day retrospective threat hunting, forensic investigations, and IOC correlation across distributed environments. SIEM/SOAR integration, YARA scanning, and remote live response help SOC teams accelerate containment and reduce dwell time. Most enterprise security teams can describe their managed endpoints accurately. They struggle to account for everything that is actively connecting to corporate resources right now. Contractor laptops with no MDM enrollment. BYOD devices accessing SaaS platforms through personal networks. Remote employee workstations that have not touched the corporate VPN in two weeks. Shared lab machines with no agent. All of these are live access points. Most generate no telemetry, no behavioral data, and no alerts. The 2025 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report [1] , which analyzed over 22,000 security incidents, found that infostealers compromised 46% of unmanaged devices holding company credentials. Third-party device involvement in breaches doubled year over year, reaching 30% of all confirmed cases. Credential abuse and vulnerability exploitation together drove 42% of initial breach vectors. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report [2] puts the global average breach cost at $4.44 million, with U.S. organizations hitting a record $10.22 million per incident. Those numbers trace back to one root cause: endpoints that security teams cannot see cannot generate the alerts that stop attacks. This guide covers the Fidelis EDR deployment strategy for these environments specifically. Architecture, deployment phases, detection engineering, incident response workflows, and SIEM/SOAR integration. Written for security architects, SOC leads, and CISOs evaluating endpoint detection and response for a distributed, hybrid workforce. Why Traditional Antivirus Software Fails Against Modern Endpoint Threats Two separate problems make legacy endpoint security inadequate for remote and unmanaged environments. The first is detection architecture. The second is network dependency. Both need to be understood before evaluating any EDR deployment strategy. Signature-Based Detection Cannot Stop What It Has Never Seen Traditional antivirus software is built around one assumption: someone already identified the threat and generated a signature. Against modern sophisticated attacks, that model fails structurally. The Picus Red Report 2026 [4] , covering analysis of 1.1 million malware samples, found that 80% of the top ten MITRE ATT&CK techniques actively used in attacks focus specifically on defense evasion. Fileless malware executes entirely in memory using native Windows tools: PowerShell, WMI, certutil.exe, mshta.exe. Nothing lands on disk. Signature scanners have nothing to match. Ponemon Institute research confirmed that fileless attacks are ten times more likely to succeed than file-based attacks. Traditional antivirus software generates zero alert for these techniques because there is no file to scan. Living-off-the-land (LOTL) attacks extend that evasion further. Attackers use legitimate Windows binaries to move laterally, escalate privileges, and establish persistence. Every process involved is a native OS tool. Detecting this class of attack requires behavioral analysis of process context, parent-child relationships, command line arguments, and outbound network connections. Capabilities that endpoint protection platforms built on signature matching simply do not provide. The 2025 Verizon DBIR confirmed that vulnerability exploitation surged 34% year over year. VPN appliances and edge devices were specifically called out as primary targets. Traditional security measures address none of this effectively. VPN-Dependent EDR Tools Leave Remote Endpoints Exposed Many first-generation EDR tools assume managed network access. The agent sends telemetry through a corporate-controlled path. Detection logic runs server-side. When the endpoint goes off-network, the agent goes partially blind. Events queue. Detection gaps open. For remote employees on home networks, contractors on personal ISPs, and traveling staff across time zones, that architecture creates exactly the window attackers exploit. An endpoint compromised while off-VPN may not surface detection events until it reconnects. By then, data exfiltration may already be complete and lateral movement already executed. CISA’s 2025 [3] Year in Review documented that in FY2025, the agency scaled endpoint detection and response deployment to more than 60 federal agencies covering over 500,000 endpoints through its Persistent Access Capability program. The explicit reason cited: continuous on-device visibility is a prerequisite for detecting advanced persistent threats in near real time. That requirement applies equally to enterprise environments. Faster Threat Investigations Start with Deeper Endpoint Visibility Establish Deep Telemetry Enable Timeline-Based Investigation Continuously Validate Endpoint Visibility Read the Guide Fidelis Endpoint ® Architecture: Built for Off-Network and Unmanaged Environments Understanding how Fidelis Endpoint ® is built explains why it handles remote and unmanaged environments where other tools fall short. The architecture has three core components: the agent itself, the Endpoint Collector, and the telemetry it gathers. Single Lightweight Agent, On-Grid and Off-Grid Detection Fidelis Endpoint ® deploys one lightweight agent across Windows, macOS, and Linux. No VPN connection is required for detection to function. Threat intelligence and detection logic are pushed locally to the agent at deployment. Detections fire on-device regardless of network state. When an endpoint loses connectivity, the agent continues monitoring locally, caches events and queued jobs, and syncs everything to the Endpoint Collector once reconnection occurs. A remote employee targeted by a phishing-delivered macro while on a hotel network still triggers detection. The behavioral pattern was observed on-device. The alert fires. Response can begin as soon as the device reconnects or while it is still isolated. Agent-to-server communication uses TLS 1.2 encrypted WebSocket connections. The channel is persistent and lightweight by design, avoiding meaningful competition with business application traffic on bandwidth-constrained connections. Endpoint Collector: Centralized Behavioral Telemetry Store Every agent feeds into the Endpoint Collector, a centralized repository for endpoint behavioral metadata. The Collector stores process starts and stops, parent-child process relationships, registry reads and writes, file creation and modification events, DNS lookups, HTTP and HTTPS connections, network socket activity, and Windows Event Log entries. Retention is configurable at 30, 60, or 90 days. NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC 2.0 Level 2 guidance specifies a 90-day minimum telemetry retention baseline for audit and incident response requirements. Fidelis matches that directly. The stored metadata enables retrospective analysis . When a threat surfaces today, analysts query what happened on any endpoint 60 days ago without depending on SIEM log completeness or network tap coverage. What the Fidelis Agent Collects Per Endpoint Telemetry Category Data Captured Process Activity Start/stop, command line arguments, parent PID, file hash File System Created, written, modified, closed, deleted events Registry Key reads, writes, deletions Network DNS queries, HTTP/HTTPS, remote IPs, socket connections Windows Events Logon events, account changes, service installations Memory Loaded DLLs, injected threads, process memory state Executables and Scripts First-seen copy of every binary and script executed The executable and script collection deserves specific attention. Fidelis saves a copy of every binary and script the first time it executes anywhere in the environment. Attackers routinely delete tools post-execution. With this collection active, analysts retain the sample for hash analysis, threat intelligence correlation, and cross-environment scoping, even after the attacker has cleaned up on the endpoint. Fidelis EDR Deployment Process: Five Phases to Full Coverage Deploying Fidelis Endpoint ® across a mixed environment of managed, remote, and unmanaged devices follows a predictable sequence. Skipping phases or rushing through them is how coverage gaps persist. Each phase builds on the one before it. Phase 1: Endpoint Inventory and Risk Tiering Pull authentication logs from your identity provider. Every device that authenticated to corporate resources in the past 90 days is in scope. Cross-reference that list against MDM enrollment records and your current EDR coverage map. The gap between those three datasets is your actual unmanaged endpoint exposure, and it is almost always larger than asset inventory reflects. Prioritize deployment by risk tier: systems with access to sensitive data or production infrastructure first, remote worker endpoints second, contractor and shared devices after that. Why Traditional Antivirus Software Fails Against Modern Endpoint Threats

Two separate problems make legacy endpoint security inadequate for remote and unmanaged environments. The first is detection architecture. The second is network dependency. Both need to be understood before evaluating any EDR deployment strategy.

Signature-Based Detection Cannot Stop What It Has Never Seen

Traditional antivirus software is built around one assumption: someone already identified the threat and generated a signature. Against modern sophisticated attacks, that model fails structurally.

The Picus Red Report 2026[4], covering analysis of 1.1 million malware samples, found that 80% of the top ten MITRE ATT&CK techniques actively used in attacks focus specifically on defense evasion. Fileless malware executes entirely in memory using native Windows tools: PowerShell, WMI, certutil.exe, mshta.exe. Nothing lands on disk. Signature scanners have nothing to match. Ponemon Institute research confirmed that fileless attacks are ten times more likely to succeed than file-based attacks. Traditional antivirus software generates zero alert for these techniques because there is no file to scan.

Living-off-the-land (LOTL) attacks extend that evasion further. Attackers use legitimate Windows binaries to move laterally, escalate privileges, and establish persistence. Every process involved is a native OS tool. Detecting this class of attack requires behavioral analysis of process context, parent-child relationships, command line arguments, and outbound network connections. Capabilities that endpoint protection platforms built on signature matching simply do not provide.

The 2025 Verizon DBIR confirmed that vulnerability exploitation surged 34% year over year. VPN appliances and edge devices were specifically called out as primary targets. Traditional security measures address none of this effectively.

VPN-Dependent EDR Tools Leave Remote Endpoints Exposed

Many first-generation EDR tools assume managed network access. The agent sends telemetry through a corporate-controlled path. Detection logic runs server-side. When the endpoint goes off-network, the agent goes partially blind. Events queue. Detection gaps open.

For remote employees on home networks, contractors on personal ISPs, and traveling staff across time zones, that architecture creates exactly the window attackers exploit. An endpoint compromised while off-VPN may not surface detection events until it reconnects. By then, data exfiltration may already be complete and lateral movement already executed.

CISA’s 2025[3] Year in Review documented that in FY2025, the agency scaled endpoint detection and response deployment to more than 60 federal agencies covering over 500,000 endpoints through its Persistent Access Capability program. The explicit reason cited: continuous on-device visibility is a prerequisite for detecting advanced persistent threats in near real time. That requirement applies equally to enterprise environments.

Fidelis Endpoint® Architecture: Built for Off-Network and Unmanaged Environments

Understanding how Fidelis Endpoint® is built explains why it handles remote and unmanaged environments where other tools fall short. The architecture has three core components: the agent itself, the Endpoint Collector, and the telemetry it gathers.

Single Lightweight Agent, On-Grid and Off-Grid Detection

Fidelis Endpoint® deploys one lightweight agent across Windows, macOS, and Linux. No VPN connection is required for detection to function. Threat intelligence and detection logic are pushed locally to the agent at deployment. Detections fire on-device regardless of network state.

When an endpoint loses connectivity, the agent continues monitoring locally, caches events and queued jobs, and syncs everything to the Endpoint Collector once reconnection occurs. A remote employee targeted by a phishing-delivered macro while on a hotel network still triggers detection. The behavioral pattern was observed on-device. The alert fires. Response can begin as soon as the device reconnects or while it is still isolated.

Agent-to-server communication uses TLS 1.2 encrypted WebSocket connections. The channel is persistent and lightweight by design, avoiding meaningful competition with business application traffic on bandwidth-constrained connections.

Endpoint Collector: Centralized Behavioral Telemetry Store

Every agent feeds into the Endpoint Collector, a centralized repository for endpoint behavioral metadata. The Collector stores process starts and stops, parent-child process relationships, registry reads and writes, file creation and modification events, DNS lookups, HTTP and HTTPS connections, network socket activity, and Windows Event Log entries.

Retention is configurable at 30, 60, or 90 days. NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC 2.0 Level 2 guidance specifies a 90-day minimum telemetry retention baseline for audit and incident response requirements. Fidelis matches that directly.

The stored metadata enables retrospective analysis. When a threat surfaces today, analysts query what happened on any endpoint 60 days ago without depending on SIEM log completeness or network tap coverage.

Detection coverage in Fidelis Endpoint® comes from three distinct mechanisms, each addressing a different threat class. Knowing when to use which is what separates effective detection engineering from a system that either misses too much or generates too much noise.

IOC-based detection catches known threats at speed. A confirmed hash, IP, or domain correlates against endpoint telemetry in milliseconds. Behavior rules detect attacks based on what they do, not what they are. A rule that flags any PowerShell process spawning a child that connects outbound to a non-corporate IP catches a wide range of malware families without knowing their specific indicators. That detection logic holds when attackers rotate C2 infrastructure and change payloads, because the behavioral pattern persists across variants.

Apply YARA rules to scan executables pre-execution. For organizations where replacing an existing AV investment requires a multi-quarter procurement process, Fidelis EDR adds prevention capability now without waiting for that cycle to complete.
